content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes techniques to update Bayesian neural networks (with respect to a few additional training points) in a computationally efficient way. These techniques are evaluated for calibration, generalization performance, and OOD detection. Furthermore, an application of the techniques and experiments are given for batch active learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
 - The empirical results are slightly positive, though it is perhaps worrying that the fast update improves the accuracy and NLL by half as much as retraining (for SNGP-LA, the best performing method).
 - The experimental results for active learning are quite good.
 - The batching technique for active learning is clever.

Weaknesses:
 - I'm less familiar with the Bayesian neural network literature, but to make the paper more self-contained and complete, it would be nice to work out some of the mathematical details such as the derivation of equation (10) and possibly equation (15). If space doesn't permit in the main paper, at least in the appendix.
 - It is not clear what parts of the method (section 3.2) are claimed as novel vs existing work.
 - I think that the difficult sections could use more explanation while other simpler sections could be more succinct. For example, a lot of explanation is given for basic Bayesian concepts while more advanced techniques (several for "LA-based Bayesian Updates") sometimes only receive a couple sentences. I think a similar comment can be made for experiments and discussion.
 - The datasets (especially LETTER and PDIGITS which are less common) could use a brief description.
 - The active learning experiments (Figure F.1) are in a low accuracy regime for FMNIST (below 85% and should at least be low 90's percent). This might be corrected by increasing the budget. Also, this might show separation between the different active learning strategies.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality and clarity of the paper is alright. As mentioned above, the contribution is not clear and the paper is not very self-contained. 

As I am less familiar with the Bayesian neural network literature, I cannot comment on the originality.
content.summary_of_the_review: I do not recommend this paper be accepted due to (1) the structure of writing (where words are spent) could be improved (related to self-containment comment), and (2) the originality is unclear. I don't think the empirical results are strong enough to outweigh these concerns.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a fast Bayesian update method to update the predictions with additional data without retraining the Bayesian neural networks. To this end, the paper derives various formulas to perform Bayesian updates based on different mechanisms including Monte Carlo sampling and las-layer Laplace approximation. Experimental evaluation is conducted using various tabular and image datasets including LETTER, PDIGITS, MNIST, FMNIST to understand the efficacy of the proposed Bayesian update technique. Besides, a use case for active learning with the proposed Bayesian update technique is also conducted to show the practicality of the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ Overall, I think the paper targets an interesting, important, and difficult problem.
+ I appreciate all the formulas derived for the proposed Bayesian update technique.
+ The discussion and analysis around the experimental results are also interesting and detailed. Finally, the paper writing is very clear and easy to understand. 

Weaknesses: I have various concerns regarding the practicality of the proposed technique. Please see below my main concerns.
+ The formulas derived for Bayesian updates are based on various ideal assumptions, such as the posterior distribution p(\omega|D) is computed accurately, but in practice, this is not the case. There are various factors that are not ideal in practice, for example, the prediction and uncertainty generated by MC-based BNN or LA-based BNN are not accurate, or the hyper-parameters used to train the BNN models are not known or can't be found accurately given a small number of training data. Note that I'm generally okay with a method developed by using some ideal assumptions, but in this case, extensive experiments need to be conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed technique. In the paper, the experimental evaluation only uses some simple and easy datasets (LETTER, PDIGITS, MNIST, FMNIST), so it's hard to see if the proposed method can work in more complicated scenarios. I expect more evaluation on more complex datasets to be conducted.

+ For a standard retraining method, apart from retraining the model, we can always re-tune the hyperparameters so as to improve the accuracy of a DL model. With the proposed Bayesian update technique, I really doubt that we can re-use the existing hyperparameters with the new update data and still ensure the new model has high accuracy. Unless I missed it, but the paper does not mention anything about this aspect. How can we choose the hyperparameters for the BNN models and do we need to adjust these hyperparameters when there are new updated data?
+ In the experiments, the size of the updated data is only 32, this is too small, I don't think we can see any clear effect of the proposed Bayesian update technique and the standard retraining technique with this size. I expect more evaluation with larger sizes of the updated data.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4640 by Reviewer gkXW

content.title: Response to gkXW
content.comment:
Thanks for your review and positive feedback regarding our paper's readability and presentation of experimental results. In the following, we will address each potential weakness individually.

- We agree that BNNs provide only approximations (with varying accuracy) to the true posterior distribution. However, our paper investigates that by comparing three different BNNs types, which approximate the posterior distribution with different assumptions. We experimentally showed that only SNGP provides sufficiently good approximations for updating. To investigate that further, we could include other BNN types, such as Prior Networks [1] or Bayes-by-Backprop [2]. We also agree that more complex datasets and models are needed to validate our approach's effectiveness. However, as mentioned in our paper, such an update will have less impact on large network architectures or complex datasets. We will investigate this issue for future revisions.
- That is a critical point and difficult to answer. Generally, one can use an initial set to tune hyperparameters through a grid search. However, this will not guarantee a well-working model or update throughout the continual learning process. To the best of our knowledge, this is ongoing research (see section 7 in [3]) and beyond the scope of our paper.
- We agree. We will investigate the influence of the number of samples used for updating as an additional part of our ablation study.

[1] Osband, Ian, John Aslanides, and Albin Cassirer. "Randomized prior functions for deep reinforcement learning." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 31 (2018).

[2] Blundell, Charles, et al. "Weight uncertainty in neural network." *International conference on machine learning*. PMLR, 2015.

[3] Mai, Zheda, et al. "Online continual learning in image classification: An empirical survey." *Neurocomputing* 469 (2022): 28-51.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents Bayesian updates for three types of Bayesian neural networks (ensemble, dropout, and SNGP) as an alternative to complete re-training. The Bayesian updates on those BNNs are simple and fast. The authors analyze the methods’ generalization, probability calibration, and out-of-distribution detection on tabular data and grey image data. It also shows the effectiveness of Bayesian updates in an active learning case.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Most of the paper is clearly written, and the method explanation is easy to follow. 
- The visualization states the method behavior very well.
- The proposed method is simple and interesting.

Weaknesses:
- The method section only describes the Bayesian updates with only one update. But Bayesian updates can incorporate multiple updates. The method can get more general by mentioning the generic multiple update case.
- I feel the active learning-related work can be shortened or removed as only one application mentions active learning strategies. 
- The traditional Bayesian update, which updates the whole network, is a very relevant baseline besides re-training. Experiments can add this baseline (e.g., Laplace Propagation or Bayes by Backprop) to emphasize the “fast” update.
- The image dataset in the experiments only involves simple grey images and lacks diversity. Trying out the method on CIFAR10 can make the work more convincing.
- While reading section 5, I didn’t understand how the experiments are conducted and what it demonstrates. Adding more demonstrations and explanations could be helpful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The majority of the paper is well written, and the main method is very easy to grasp by looking at the figures.  Some experiments lack details to understand the procedure and purpose.

Suggestions:
- The introduction and related work section mention that the authors are interested in the catastrophic forgetting phenomenon. However, I didn’t find any experiment that reflects that part.
- The experiment only involves one update case but can possibly be extended to multiple updates.

Two more questions:
- Maybe a trivial question, is the “fast” relative to conventional Bayesian update? If not, how does it compare to conventional Bayesian updates (repeated as the second point in the above Weaknesses)?
- How does the posterior sample size of Ensemble and Dropout affect the performance?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper can improve the generality of its method by extending to multiple updates in theory and experiments. For experiments, the paper only uses one baseline – complete re-training. However, there is a gap between the re-training baseline and the last-layer update method: the traditional Bayesian update, which updates the whole network. The distinction between the proposed fast update and the traditional Bayesian updates is not clarified; only related work mentioned the difference a little. More experiments or explanations are needed in that regard. The authors can still refine some parts of the related work and experiments. The paper still has room for improvement in my opinion.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Bayesian approach for updating neural networks in a continual learning setting. The proposed method is applied to BNNs based on sampling/ensembles and Laplace approximation. The effectiveness of the method is evaluated in classification and active learning settings, as well as by assessing the calibration and quality of uncertainty for out-of-distribution detection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper focus on an interesting and relevant problem. It is well organized and easy to follow and the authors provide their code, which is also a positve aspect. However, there are several flaws in the paper: 1. In the introduction, the use of Bayesian neural networks is partially motivated by enabling to update the model with aditional data. It is not clear, however, why other continual learning approaches are not a viable alternative, as they also allow to update the model in an incremental fashion, with new data arriving sequentially. 2. In the introduction, it is stated that _"BNNs, together with our Bayesian updates, do not require batch strategies and can immediately make use of use the new labels"_. However, BNNs strategies (including the ones used in this paper) are often trained with minibatches and full-batch training of BNNs is very challenging for large scale datasets [1]. Moreover, it is, again, not clear why other continual learning approaches cannot make use of the new labels. 3. In Section 3.2, for the updates for MC-based methods, it is assumed that the posterior distribution of the models assigns uniform distribution to all weights, which is used to initialize the approximate distribution as $q(w|\mathcal{D}) = \frac{1}{M}$. There is no evidence or theoretical support for this statement. In fact, if the posterior distribution was uniform (as suggested), training BNNs would be trivial. 4. In the same section, the approximate posterior update, $q(w_m | \mathcal{D} \cup \mathcal{D}^\oplus)$, is given as a normalization over the $M$ sampled models. There is no evidence provided of why this would give the correct probability distribution, particularly if we consider the use of the uniform distribution for $p(w|\mathcal{D})$. 5. The results presented in Figure 2 shows the Bayesian update technique leading to a much more overconfident estimation of the probabilities (with less uncertainty around the decision boundary), which indicates a poor quality estimation of uncertainties. This should be discussed and evaluated in more detail. 6. The choice of evaluating calibration by comparing negative log-likelihood (NLL) is odd, as there are more appropriate metrics, such as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) proposed in the paper cited by the authors [2]. In particular, an overconfident (and thus poorly calibrated) can present a lower NLL, so the metric doesn't reflect well the calibration. 7. The evaluation presented in the paper is also lacking in terms of baselines. The results presented are contrasted only against retraining the network from scratch with the two datasets. In this context, it is expected that any reasonable attempt of learning with $\mathcal{D}^\oplus$ would be better than not using it at all and worse than retraining with the whole data. The lack of comparison with other baselines or other methods that perform continual learning diminishes the impact of the presented results. See [3-5] for some examples. 8. Another strange aspect is the miniscule dataset sizes used (with the original dataset having at most 320 datapoints). And the new dataset $\mathcal{D}^\oplus$ is similar to what a single batch of data would be in common settings. I don't understand why such small sizes are used, in particular when the datasets used have dozens of thousands of examples. [1]: Izmailov, P., Vikram, S., Hoffman, M.D. & Wilson, A.G.G.. (2021). What Are Bayesian Neural Network Posteriors Really Like?. Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 139:4629-4640 https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/izmailov21a.html. [2]: Guo, C., Pleiss, G., Sun, Y. & Weinberger, K.Q.. (2017). On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 70:1321-1330 https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html. [3]: H. Li, P. Barnaghi, S. Enshaeifar and F. Ganz, "Continual Learning Using Bayesian Neural Networks," in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, vol. 32, no. 9, pp. 4243-4252, Sept. 2021, doi: 10.1109/TNNLS.2020.3017292. [4]: Du, X., Venkataramanaiah, S. K., Li, Z., Suh, H. S., Yin, S., Krishnan, G., ... & Cao, Y. (2022). Efficient Continual Learning at the Edge with Progressive Segmented Training. Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering. [5]: Ebrahimi, S., Elhoseiny, M., Darrell, T., & Rohrbach, M. (2020). Uncertainty-guided continual learning with bayesian neural networks. International Conference on Learning Representations.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:**
The paper is well organized and easy to read for the most part.

**Quality:** 
The paper has major flaws in the theoretical justification and the empirical experimentation. Some of the formulations (e.g. assuming uniform posterior distributions) are unjustified and produce a biased estimator. And the proposed method is not compared with any other alternative method for continual learning, the dataset sizes used are very small and the evaluation of calibration and uncertainty quantification is poorly done.

**Novelty:**
The paper lacks in novelty. The strategies employed for the Bayesian updates proposed are derived from pre-existing work and the only novelty is the combination of existing prior work.

**Reproducibility:**
While there are implementation details which are not explicitly given in the text (e.g. details about the dataset split), the authors provide code, which allows for reproducing the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper propose a simple way of updating BNNs in a continual learning setting, by re-weighting samples or updating a Gaussian estimation with the new data points. However, there are significant flaws in the methodology and the evaluation is lacking, with missing baselines, improper metrics and strange choices of using only tiny subsets of datasets. For this reason, I cannot recommend acceptance.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4640 by Reviewer Wgk8

content.title: Response to Wgk8
content.comment:
Thanks for your review and positive feedback regarding our paper's structure and readability. In the following, we will address each potential flaw individually.

1. The development of our approach was originally motivated by an active learning perspective, where we make updates with relatively small batches of data (even for single samples) and a focus on reliable uncertainty estimates. Thus, we proposed to use SNGP with only last-layer updates. However, we agree that we should revise our paper to consider also state-of-the-art continual learning approaches.
2. In our paper and all experiments, we still train our models via mini-batches. Your cited statement does not refer to the general training of our BNN but relates exclusively to the Bayesian updates in the context of active learning. There, humans label samples successively, and we want to update our BNN for each newly labeled sample individually.
3. From our point of view, there is a misconception regarding MC samples from your side. The uniform weighting of drawn MC samples does not imply that the underlying posterior distribution is uniform. The intuition behind this is that MC samples in high-density regions are drawn more frequently and thus (despite the equal weighting) are more strongly represented. Classical BNN literature typically assumes this when the predictive distribution is approximated by MC integration (cf. page 5 after Algorithm 1 in [1]).
4. As all distributions in Eq. 5 are categorical, the resulting distribution will also be categorical. The product in Eq. 5 can be seen as unnormalized importance weights, as also mentioned in [2]. We will revise the appendix and add a more detailed derivation.
5. We agree with your statement that the update for Ensemble and MC-Dropout lead to a much more overconfident estimation. However, one of the key messages we wanted to show is that proper modeling of uncertainty in the baseline model is an essential requirement for our Bayesian updating technique to work. In the revision of our paper, we will highlight this.
6. The evaluation of calibration with NLL is commonly done in the literature [3] as it is a proper scoring rule (the optimum score corresponds to a perfect prediction). We did not use the suggested ECE as trivial solutions yield optimal scores. For the sake of completeness, we will include the ECE in the revision of the paper.
7. We agree and will include the suggested baselines in the revision.
8. As the used datasets have low complexity, increasing the number of samples would lead to an almost perfect model. In such a scenario, further updating is not needed. To make this more apparent, we will increase the number of maximum samples.

**Regarding the Novelty:**

The proposed method is indeed a combination of existing works. However, we believe that the concept of second-order Bayesian updates for computing the maximum a posterior parameters in the context of deep learning is new. This way, we obtain significant changes in the output of a model with very small sample sizes and few optimization steps.

Furthermore, we empirically show which requirements (e.g., proper uncertainty modeling) are crucial for BNNs so that Bayesian updates work.

Another novelty is the combination of Bayesian updates with sequential active learning strategies as an alternative to batch strategies.

[1] Lakshminarayanan, Balaji, Alexander Pritzel, and Charles Blundell. "Simple and scalable predictive uncertainty estimation using deep ensembles." *Advances in neural information processing systems* 30 (2017).

[2] Kirsch, Andreas, Jannik Kossen, and Yarin Gal. "Marginal and Joint Cross-Entropies & Predictives for Online Bayesian Inference, Active Learning, and Active Sampling." *arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.08766* (2022).

[3] Ovadia, Yaniv, et al. "Can you trust your model's uncertainty? evaluating predictive uncertainty under dataset shift." *Advances in neural information processing systems* 32 (2019).

Accordingly, mentioning revision in the review responses refers to future venues.
